## Results

### Data Set and Workflow

Across the 3 validation reviews, 6,214 bibliographic records were retrieved from PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library and processed sequentially through deduplication, title and abstract screening, full-text screening, and structured data extraction.

### Deduplication Performance

The deduplication agent identified 1,025 duplicate records using DOI matching, title similarity, and author/year concordance. Against human reviewers, accuracy was 98.7% with Cohen’s κ = 0.98, indicating almost perfect agreement comparable with established reference management tools. In cases of uncertainty, duplicates were retained to avoid inadvertent exclusion (Table I).

### Title and Abstract Screening

Of 5,189 records subjected to title and abstract screening, reviewers excluded 4,861 records based on eligibility criteria, of which the AI agent correctly excluded 98.5%. The dual-pass strategy yielded κ = 0.91 (0.89-0.93) vs. human reviewers, reflecting strong concordance, and reduced records requiring full-text review by 92% (Table I). Robustness was enhanced through cross-validation and stratified sampling, with outputs partitioned by publication year and independently adjudicated against human ground truth.

### Full-Text Screening

Full-text screening was conducted exclusively by human reviewers. The screening agent forwarded 399 records vs. the 329 reviewers would have forwarded—a deliberate overinclusion of 70 records (21.3%) reflecting a sensitivity-weighted threshold, as false negatives at title/abstract screening are unrecoverable while false positives are inexpensive to remove at full-text adjudication. All 70 additional records were excluded on full-text review, confirming the overinclusion did not compromise the evidence base. Of the 329 records reviewers progressed, 72 met the inclusion criteria.

### Structured Data Extraction

The extraction agent processed the 72 included studies, capturing 1,550 structured data fields (sample sizes, binary outcomes, and continuous measures with SDs). Dual-pass extraction yielded κ = 0.87 (0.86-0.88) with 93% concordance vs. human reviewers, representing substantial agreement. Justification logs were generated for 6.7% of entries with missing or ambiguous data—most often absent SDs, merged table cells, or incomplete subgroup reporting—all directed to human adjudication.

### Verification and Human Oversight

The verification agent flagged 104 discrepancies across deduplication, screening, and extraction, all reviewed by dual independent adjudicators with consensus in every case. Audit trails confirmed no fabricated data were introduced, and every extracted element was traceable to its source. Of the 104, 15 were critical (0.9% of total data fields extracted)—for example, swapped cohorts (intervention vs. control mislabeling) or misinterpreted composite outcomes—and were corrected by human reviewers.

### Time Efficiency

The framework reduced reviewer time by 91.1% (90.8%-91.4%), a mean saving of 19.9 hours per review (p < 0.001), most pronounced in the data extraction phase (Table I).

### Error Classification

Minor discrepancies accounted for 86% of flagged outputs (formatting inconsistencies, ambiguous abbreviations, or incomplete metadata), while clinically critical errors (14%; 0.9% of total outputs) typically involved mislabeled cohorts, incorrect denominators, or omitted adverse events—for example, misclassifying “revision surgery” as a primary rather than secondary end point. These were consistently identified by the verification agent and resolved through human adjudication, underscoring the necessity of the human-in-the-loop design.

## Methods

### Deduplication benchmark datasets

We collected datasets from already executed real-life systematic searches with multiple databases (Table 1). Two different libraries (Public Health & Primary Care Library and Medical Library) performing systematic searches within the University of Bern provided the datasets. The average dataset size was 8078 references. The largest dataset contained 18,314 collected references, while the smallest dataset contained 45 manually collected references. Six datasets (healthy aging, healthy lifestyle, menopause onset, hypertension, e3_gsm, and jugular) contained pooled publications (bibliographic and clinical trial metadata) within the same file.

Table 1 Description of datasets used for deduplication analysis

To collect an adequate coverage of scientific evidence, we ran exhaustive searches on multiple databases (Table 1). Each database search contributed a unique set of references; as expected, the combination of searches resulted in high overlap among retrieved references [5]. 
### Evaluation method

We compared the algorithm performance with a standardized manual deduplication process using the eight heterogeneous datasets of diverse sizes and research topics. The experts provided us with their datasets, part of executed real-world systematic searches in the past, comprised of metadata from either publications and clinical trials, or a mix of both. For each dataset, duplicates were removed by the experts using the manual deduplication process described earlier. We ran a validation process for each of the eight datasets with goals as follows:

  1. i)

Find and eliminate the maximum number of duplicates from already manually deduplicated datasets.

  2. ii)

Find erroneously removed unique references and add them back into the validated datasets.

Our validation process resulted in eight benchmark—or gold standard—datasets to compare the efficiency of deduplicating manually vs. deduplicating with Deduklick.

To find additional duplicates and avoid missing false positives (removing unique references unintentionally) and false negatives (remaining duplicates in manually deduplicated datasets), we set low thresholds (\({\theta }_{g}\ge 58\)) in Deduklick for each of the eight manually deduplicated datasets, where g represents the threshold set to find the gold standard (i.e., find bigger clusters of possible lexically similar references). --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Abstract

The study uses different types of responsibility and their linguistic manifestations as discourse analytic tools to get at a deeper understanding of a highly atypical genre: the last statements by inmates in Texas who are about to be executed. The data consist of transcribed last statements (a corpus of about 48,000 words) from the period 1982–2021, during which 573 executions took place in Texas. We discuss the different kinds of expressions of taking or neglecting to take (full or partial) responsibility for one’s deeds.
